For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the cabbage came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-cabbage" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-cabbage-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of cabbage, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

<a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach cabbage

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach cabbage comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Cabbage, as sold from Ruschita (mining area R) (mining-affected area) had lead higher at 900 µg/kg, against 50 µg/kg for Borlova (reference area) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Iosif Gergen, Monica Harmanescu · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca">Application of principal component analysis in the pollution assessment with heavy metals of vegetable food chain in the old mining areas</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemistry Central Journal6:156</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, cabbage, as sold from Ruschita old mining area (R) (mining-affected area) had lead higher at 900 µg/kg, against 50 µg/kg for Borlova reference area (Ref) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/harmanescu2011-banat-mining-vegetables-metals|20]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Harmanescu M, Alda LM, Bordean DM, Gogoasa I, Gergen I · 2011</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/harmanescu2011-banat-mining-vegetables-metals">Heavy metals health risk assessment for population via consumption of vegetables grown in old mining area; a case study: Banat County, Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemistry Central Journal 2011, 5:64</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/harmanescu2011-banat-mining-vegetables-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

<a id="additional-geographic-and-remediation-evidence"></a>
<a id="mitigation-options"></a>
## Mitigation for cabbage

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>
<a id="under-what-conditions-at-which-stage-and-against-which-comparator-do-they-work-or-fail"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-021"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-field-or-commercial-implementation-and-ongoing-verification"></a>

Lot testing against the applicable limit is the check that can be verified.

<p class="hmi-mitigation-gap" data-mitigation-gap>No measured way to lower metals in this food is in the library yet.</p>



<a id="trade-offs-and-failure-modes"></a>
## Trade-offs and limits of controls

<a id="hmi-ing-022"></a>
<a id="can-an-intervention-increase-another-contaminant-or-redistribute-contamination-to-a-by-product"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-023"></a>
<a id="what-effects-on-nutrition-yield-sensory-quality-stability-and-waste-streams-were-measured"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-024"></a>
<a id="what-costs-constraints-adverse-effects-or-failure-modes-are-documented-and-which-are-unknown"></a>

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Iosif Gergen, Monica Harmanescu · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca">Application of principal component analysis in the pollution assessment with heavy metals of vegetable food chain in the old mining areas</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemistry Central Journal6:156</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.



<a id="sampling-and-testing"></a>
## Testing cabbage for metals

<a id="hmi-ing-025"></a>
<a id="what-sampling-design-is-appropriate-for-the-ingredient-heterogeneity-lot-and-decision"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-026"></a>
<a id="which-methods-species-measurements-validation-evidence-and-reporting-limits-are-needed"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-027"></a>
<a id="what-can-a-certificate-of-analysis-or-non-detect-establish-and-what-remains-untested"></a>

Results depend on the method and its reporting limit. Reporting limits for lead ranged from 0.5 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 10,000 µg/kg (Sultana et al. 2022), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup <a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Cabbage FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-cabbage" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-cabbage" data-question="What heavy metals are found in cabbage?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in cabbage?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, total mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, antimony, uranium, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, Se, Ag, As, Ba, Hg, Mo, Sr, Ti and Tl in cabbage, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" assessment</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxin Reviews</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/alimohammadi2018-tehran-supermarket-vegetables">Read <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-cabbage" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-cabbage" data-question="How do heavy metals get into cabbage?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into cabbage?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, cabbage from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than cabbage from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Iosif Gergen, Monica Harmanescu · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca">Application of principal component analysis in the pollution assessment with heavy metals of vegetable food chain in the old mining areas</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemistry Central Journal6:156</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Cabbage, as sold from Moldova Noua (mining area M) (mining-affected area) had lead higher at 250 µg/kg, against 50 µg/kg for Borlova (reference area) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Iosif Gergen, Monica Harmanescu · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca">Application of principal component analysis in the pollution assessment with heavy metals of vegetable food chain in the old mining areas</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Chemistry Central Journal6:156</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gergen2012-banat-mining-vegetable-pca">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-cabbage" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-cabbage" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in cabbage?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in cabbage?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, cabbage, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (2.3 µg/kg) and the highest in PAHO (185 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in EURO (3.88 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (195 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-cabbage-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-cabbage-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in cabbage is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in cabbage is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 11 results from 3 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fera2015-uk-tds-metals|27]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Baxter M, Brereton N · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" Agency report for the UK Food Standards Agency, Fera report 15/06, project FS102081</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fera2015-uk-tds-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic|28]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Centre for Food Safety FEHD HKSAR · 2012</span><a
